exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude

question.text: Suppose that $|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=4$, $|\,\mathbf{b}\,|=8\sqrt{2}$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\mathbf{a}$ in terms of the vector $\mathbf{a}.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{b} &= |\,\mathbf{b}\,| \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 8\sqrt{2} \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\[5pt] &= 8\sqrt{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\[5pt] &= 8 \end{align*}

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{a}\mathbin{:}$ \[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}}{|\,\mathbf{a}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{a} \]

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{b} &= \text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{u} \\[5pt] &= 8 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} \mathbf{a} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2}\:\mathbf{a} \end{align*}

question.text: Suppose that $|\,\mathbf{p}\,|=6$, $|\,\mathbf{q}\,|=12$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = 150^{\circ}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{q}$ onto $\mathbf{p}$ in terms of the vector $\mathbf{p}.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{comp}_{\mathbf{p}}\,\mathbf{q} &= |\,\mathbf{q}\,| \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 12 \cos\left(150^{\circ}\right) \\[5pt] &= 12 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= -6\sqrt{3} \end{align*}

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{p}\mathbin{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{p}}{|\,\mathbf{p}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{p}}{6} = \dfrac{1}{6} \mathbf{p} \]

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{p}}\,\mathbf{q} &= \text{comp}_{\mathbf{p}}\,\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{u} \\[5pt] &= -6\sqrt{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} \mathbf{p} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\sqrt{3}}\,\mathbf{p} \end{align*}

question.text: Suppose that $|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=16$, $|\,\mathbf{b}\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ in terms of the vector $\mathbf{b}.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} &= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 16 \cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= 16 \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= -8 \end{align*}

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{b} \]

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} &= \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u} \\[5pt] &= -8 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4}\:\mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

question.text: Suppose that $|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=6$, $|\,\mathbf{b}\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ in terms of the vector $\mathbf{b}.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} &= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 6 \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= 6 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &= 3 \end{align*}

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{b} \]

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} &= \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u} \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{b} \end{align*}

question.text: Suppose that $|\,\mathbf{c}\,|=12$, $|\,\mathbf{d}\,|=6$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{d}$ onto $\mathbf{c}$ in terms of the vector $\mathbf{c}.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{comp}_{\mathbf{c}}\,\mathbf{d} &= |\,\mathbf{d}\,| \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 6 \cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= 6 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= -3 \end{align*}

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{c}\mathbin{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{c}}{|\,\mathbf{c}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{c}}{12} = \dfrac{1}{12} \mathbf{c} \]

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{c}}\,\mathbf{d} &= \text{comp}_{\mathbf{c}}\,\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{u} \\[5pt] &= (-3) \cdot \dfrac{1}{12} \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{c} \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Vector Projection Using Components

question.text: Let $\mathbf{c}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 8 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{d}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{c}$ onto $\mathbf{d}.$
question.explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{d}}\,\mathbf{c} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}} \mathbf{d} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{c_x d_x + c_y d_y + c_z d_z}{d_x^2+d_y^2+d_z^2} \mathbf{d} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-2) \cdot (-1) + 8 \cdot 3 + (-1) \cdot (-2)}{(-1)^2+3^2+(-2)^2} \mathbf{d} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{28}{14} \langle -1,3,-2 \rangle \\[5pt] &= 2 \langle -1,3,-2 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left\langle \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-2},\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{6},\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4} \right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{c}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{d}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{d}$ onto $\mathbf{c}.$
question.explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{c}}\,\mathbf{d} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{c}} \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{c_x d_x + c_y d_y + c_z d_z}{c_x^2+c_y^2+c_z^2} \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot (-3) + (-3) \cdot 5}{2^2+1^2+(-3)^2} \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{14}{14} \langle 2,1,-3 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left\langle -2, -1, 3 \right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{c}=\langle 2,-1,6 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{d}=\langle 4,-2,10 \rangle.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{c}$ onto $\mathbf{d}.$
question.explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{d}}\,\mathbf{c} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}} \mathbf{d} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{c_x d_x + c_y d_y + c_z d_z}{d_x^2+d_y^2+d_z^2} \mathbf{d} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2 \cdot 4 + (-1) \cdot (-2) + 6 \cdot 10}{4^2+(-2)^2+10^2} \mathbf{d} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{70}{120} \langle 4,-2,10 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{7}{12} \langle 4,-2,10 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left\langle \,\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{7}{3}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{7}{6}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{35}{6}} \,\right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{c}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{d}=\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{d}$ onto $\mathbf{c}.$
question.explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{c}}\,\mathbf{d} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{c}} \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{c_x d_x + c_y d_y + c_z d_z}{c_x^2+c_y^2+c_z^2} \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-1)\cdot 4 + 2\cdot (-3) + 5\cdot 1}{(-1)^2+2^2+5^2} \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-4 - 6 + 5}{1+4+25} \,\mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{5}{30}\,\langle -1,2,5 \rangle \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{6}\,\langle -1,2,5 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left\langle \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{6}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{1}{3}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{5}{6}} \right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{r}=\langle 2,-1,3 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{s}=\langle 5,1,-4 \rangle.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{s}$ onto $\mathbf{r}.$
question.explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{r}}\,\mathbf{s} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}} \mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{r_x s_x + r_y s_y + r_z s_z}{r_x^2+r_y^2+r_z^2} \mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2 \cdot 5 + (-1) \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot (-4)}{2^2+(-1)^2+3^2} \mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{10 - 1 - 12}{4+1+9} \langle 2,-1,3 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-3}{14} \langle 2,-1,3 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left\langle \,\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{3}{7}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{14}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{9}{14}} \,\right\rangle. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Vector Projection Using Components

question.text: Let $\mathbf{a} = \langle 0, 1, -5 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle 6, x ,-2 \rangle.$ Given that the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$
question.explanation:
Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular.

So, we must have \[ \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0. \]

Computing the dot product, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} &= a_x \cdot b_x + a_y \cdot b_y + a_z \cdot b_z \\[5pt] &= 0 \cdot 6 + 1 \cdot x +(-5) \cdot (-2) \\[5pt] &= x + 10. \end{align*}

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} &= 0 \\[5pt] x + 10 &= 0 \\[5pt] x &= -10. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{a}=\langle 1, -2, 5 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 3, -1, -1 \rangle.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$
question.explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b}} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z}{b_x^2+b_y^2+b_z^2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1 \cdot 3 + (-2) \cdot (-1) + 5 \cdot (-1)}{3^2+(-1)^2+(-1)^2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{0}{3^2+(-1)^2+(-1)^2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \left\langle 0, 0, 0 \right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{u}=\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} k \\ -1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.$ Given that the projection of $\mathbf{u}$ onto $\mathbf{v}$ is the zero vector, find the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
Since $\mathbf{u}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular.

So, we must have \[ \mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0. \]

Computing the dot product, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} &= u_x \cdot v_x + u_y \cdot v_y + u_z \cdot v_z \\[5pt] &= 4 \cdot k + 2 \cdot (-1) + (-3) \cdot 5 \\[5pt] &= 4k - 2 - 15 \\[5pt] &= 4k - 17. \end{align*}

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} &= 0 \\[5pt] 4k - 17 &= 0 \\[5pt] 4k &= 17 \\[5pt] k &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{17}{4}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{a}=-2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$
question.explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

\begin{align*} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b}} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z}{b_x^2+b_y^2+b_z^2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-2) \cdot 2 + (-2) \cdot (-2) + 4 \cdot 0}{2^2+(-2)^2+0^2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{0}{2^2+(-2)^2+0^2} \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \left\langle 0, 0, 0 \right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathbf{a}=\begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ -3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ x \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Given that the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$
question.explanation:
Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular.

So, we must have \[ \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0. \]

Computing the dot product, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} &= a_x \cdot b_x + a_y \cdot b_y + a_z \cdot b_z \\[5pt] &= -6 \cdot (-2) + (-3) \cdot x + 0 \cdot (-3) \\[5pt] &= 12 -3x. \end{align*}

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} &= 0 \\[5pt] 12 - 3x &= 0 \\[5pt] -3x &= -12 \\[5pt] x &= 4. \end{align*}
